questions.q: Why is 'which option is best' often the wrong way to frame a multi-criteria architecture decision?
options: When no option wins on every axis (one is cheaper, another is faster, another is more balanced), the real question is 'best for what we actually care about, weighted how,' not a single objective answer
There is always exactly one objectively best option in every architecture decision
Multi-criteria decisions should never be made using any structured technique
Cost is always the only criterion that matters in any architecture decision
questions.explain: When options each excel on different dimensions, asking 'which is best' without specifying relative priorities skips the actual judgment call -- what matters more, and by how much.

questions.q: In the worked example, why is it significant that Options A, B, and C scored close together (7.10, 6.90, 7.00)?
options: It honestly reveals that the decision is genuinely sensitive to the chosen weights, not an obvious landslide that any reasonable weighting would reach
Close scores always indicate a calculation error
Close scores mean the weighting criteria were chosen incorrectly
Close scores have no meaningful interpretation and should be ignored
questions.explain: A close result is itself useful information -- it tells you the ranking could plausibly change under a different, equally reasonable set of weights, which is exactly why a sensitivity check matters here.

questions.q: According to the lesson, where does the real judgment call in a weighted scoring matrix actually live?
options: In the WEIGHTS assigned to each criterion (how much cost matters relative to latency, quality, maintainability) -- the scoring itself is often the more objective, measurable part
In the scoring step alone, with weights being purely arbitrary and unimportant
Neither the scores nor the weights involve any real judgment
In choosing which programming language to implement the matrix calculation in
questions.explain: Scores can often be measured relatively objectively; the weights reflect a genuine priority judgment that deserves explicit discussion, since two people can score identically and still disagree on the weights.

questions.q: How is it possible for two engineers to score every option identically on every criterion but still recommend different options?
options: They can disagree on the WEIGHTS assigned to each criterion (e.g., how much to prioritize cost vs. latency), which changes the weighted total even with identical underlying scores
This scenario is impossible -- identical scores always produce identical recommendations
One of the two engineers must have made an arithmetic error
Weighted scoring matrices always produce a unique correct answer regardless of weights
questions.explain: Identical scores combined with different weights produce different weighted totals -- which is exactly why surfacing and discussing the weights explicitly matters more than debating the scores.

questions.q: What does a sensitivity check (testing how much weights would need to change before the ranking flips) tell you about a close decision?
options: Whether the recommendation is fragile (a small weight change flips it, meaning it deserves real discussion) or robust (it holds under small weight changes, meaning the decision is more solid than it might feel)
A sensitivity check always proves the original scoring was wrong
Sensitivity checks are only useful when the top options are far apart, not when they're close
A sensitivity check replaces the need for scoring criteria entirely
questions.explain: Running a sensitivity check reveals whether a close result is fragile (worth a real priorities conversation) or robust (trustworthy despite looking close) -- valuable information either way.
